text: It depends on the task. Creative or complex projects usually benefit from a team, because people bring different skills and notice each other's mistakes. But for work that needs deep concentration, like writing or analysing data, being alone is often more efficient. The ideal is probably a mix: planning together, working separately, and then meeting again to check the results.

tips.en: It depends on the task, followed by two types of task.

text: A good leader listens more than they talk and makes sure everyone knows what they're responsible for. They also take the blame when things go wrong and share the credit when things go well. I believe these skills can be learned, especially through experience. Many people who seem like natural leaders simply had more chances to organise things when they were young.

text: For some purposes they're even better. An online lecture or conference lets thousands of people join from anywhere, without paying for travel. But they can't replace the informal side of an event — the conversations over coffee, the chance meetings that lead to new friendships or jobs. That's why I think the most successful events now combine both formats.

text: Usually because the organisers focus on how the event looks instead of who it's for. You can have an expensive venue and famous speakers, but if the timing is wrong or nobody knows about it, people won't come. For me, the most important part of planning is understanding the audience — what they want and when they're free.
